summary: The Bring Our Heroes Home Act requires federal agencies to locate, review, and publicly disclose government records relating to missing Armed Forces members and civilian personnel dating from December 7, 1941, onward. It establishes a new independent agency called the Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Review Board, along with a specialized collection at the National Archives, to manage the declassification and release of these records subject to specific national security and privacy exceptions.

affected_groups.effect: Receive expedited public access to historical records regarding the loss, fate, status, and government accounting processes concerning their missing loved ones.
affected_groups.group: Families of missing Armed Forces and civilian personnel

affected_groups.effect: Must thoroughly search, review, declassify, and transmit all records relating to missing personnel to the National Archives, submit certifications under penalty of perjury, and comply with Review Board directives.
Responsible for establishing the new records collection, preparing indexes and subject guidebooks, and making unclassified or declassified records accessible to the public.
affected_groups.group: The National Archives and Records Administration

affected_groups.effect: Operates as a new independent federal entity with subpoena and oversight powers to review postponed disclosures, employ staff, and coordinate record releases until its termination.
affected_groups.group: The Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Review Board

key_provisions: Establishes the Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Collection at the National Archives for public research and for families seeking information on missing personnel.
Creates the Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Review Board, an independent executive branch board consisting of five presidentially appointed and Senate-confirmed members.
Requires federal government offices to identify, preserve, and transmit relevant records to the Archivist, carrying a presumption of declassification unless narrow statutory exemptions apply.

Sets strict criteria and narrow exceptions under which public disclosure of records or specific information may be postponed, such as risks to national security, intelligence sources, or personal privacy.

Mandates periodic reviews of postponed records, requiring full public disclosure after 10 years unless the President certifies that continued postponement is necessary based on clear and convincing evidence of identifiable harm.
Empowers the Review Board to hold hearings, administer oaths, subpoena documents and private persons, and make final determinations on record disclosures despite agency objections.
Authorizes the appropriation of such sums as are necessary to carry out the Act, with the Review Board terminating 4 years after its members are sworn in.
missing_information: Specific dollar amounts for the authorization of appropriations to fund the Review Board and National Archives duties.
Exact timelines for when the initial quorum of Review Board members will be nominated and confirmed.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The Bring Our Heroes Home Act requires federal agencies to locate, review, and publicly disclose government records relating to missing Armed Forces members and civilian personnel dating from December 7, 1941, onward. It establishes a new independent agency called the Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Review Board, along with a specialized collection at the National Archives, to manage the declassification and release of these records subject to specific national security and privacy exceptions.
summary_detail.significance: This bill sets up a centralized federal framework with independent oversight to declassify, gather, and publicly disclose historical government records regarding missing service members and civilian personnel. By shifting the presumption toward public disclosure and overriding conflicting agency rules, it significantly alters how long-held federal records from World War II onward are made accessible to families and researchers.
